correctness.rationale: Multiplying by two gives \(n(n+1)=2^Aq^\beta\). Coprimality of consecutive factors forces the unordered pair to be \({2^A,q^\beta}\), so \(q^\beta=2^A\pm1\). The plus/minus factorizations exclude every higher exponent except the even plus-branch case \(q=3,\beta=2,A=3\); exponent one gives exactly the Fermat/Mersenne branches. The frozen verifier was read and correctly checks the reduced equations and a bounded triangular scan; the global proof is the factorization argument.

final_claim: For every fixed odd prime \(q\), all positive-exponent solutions of \(\binom{n+1}{2}=2^\alpha q^\beta\) are exactly the Mersenne branch, the Fermat branch, and the exceptional solution \((q,n,\alpha,\beta)=(3,8,2,2)\); hence the fixed support \({2,q}\) has at most two solutions, with equality only for \(q=3\).
limitations: Only fixed supports \({2,q}\) with \(q\) odd prime and positive exponents.
No claim about infinitely many Fermat or Mersenne primes.
